This is your own track, separate from your WGU degree. It has one destination: an OT threat/detection analyst or OT compliance role, and then the ICS security engineering path after that. Everything here is built for 5–7 hours a week in 15–30 minute pieces, because that is the time you actually have.

📘 DEFINITION

OT (Operational Technology): the computers that run physical things — pumps, valves, turbines, conveyor belts, chlorine dosing. If it can move something, heat something, or spill something, it is OT.

IT (Information Technology): the computers that run information — email, databases, the payroll system. Your current world.

ICS (Industrial Control System): the umbrella term for the control equipment inside OT. Used almost interchangeably with OT in job adverts.

The one deadline that actually matters

Before anything else, a date. I checked this against CompTIA's own site today, and it changes your first exam target:

★ ON THE EXAM

Security+ SY0-701 (the current version) retires around mid-May 2027. Its replacement, SY0-801, launches 17 November 2026 — about eight weeks from now.

My recommendation: sit SY0-701, and book it before May 2027. At 5–7 hours a week you will be ready around February 2027, comfortably inside the window. SY0-701 has three years of practice questions, videos and study guides behind it. SY0-801 will have almost none at launch, and you would be studying from material nobody has validated against the real exam yet. Being an early adopter costs you nothing here and buys you nothing.

How I will teach you

  1. One module at a time. I teach a module, quiz you at the end, and stop. When you say next, we move on. I will not dump six modules on you at once.
  2. Plain English first, then the technical detail. Every acronym gets defined the first time it appears — including the ones everyone assumes you know.

The mistake almost everyone makes entering OT security is studying IT security and assuming it transfers. It transfers about 60% of the way. You asked me to use your data background as a strength. It is a bigger one than you probably realise, and I want to be specific about why rather than just encouraging.

The thing OT security is actually short of

OT security has plenty of people who know plants and plenty who know IT security. What it is chronically short of is people who can look at a large volume of network data and tell what is normal. That is a data analysis problem wearing a hard hat.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Here is the thing that makes OT a gift to an analyst, and you should be able to say this sentence in an interview:

OT network traffic is boringly, beautifully predictable. An office network is chaos — people browse, stream, install things, work from cafes. A plant network does the same handful of things forever: this HMI polls that PLC for register 40001 every 500 milliseconds, all day, every day, for nine years.

That means baselining actually works in OT, where it barely works in IT. Anomaly detection in an office network drowns you in false positives. In a plant, a new source address or an unexpected function code is genuinely anomalous. Your SQL skills — group by, window functions, joins against an asset inventory — are the right tools for that job, not a transferable-skills consolation prize.

What maps directly

What you already doWhat it becomes in OT security
Writing SQL to profile a table — distinct values, counts, outliersBaselining a plant network: which devices talk to which, how often, using what function codes
GROUP BY + HAVING to find the odd rowsFinding the one engineering workstation that started writing to a PLC at 3am
Joining a fact table to a dimension tableJoining network flows to an asset inventory to spot traffic from a device that should not exist
Window functions over timeDetecting a polling interval that changed — often the first sign of a man-in-the-middle
Knowing when a dashboard is lying to youKnowing when a “normal” HMI screen is being fed replayed values — exactly what Stuxnet did
🏭 IN THE PLANT

The single most valuable OT detection skill is noticing that a value is too normal. Stuxnet recorded 21 seconds of legitimate sensor readings and replayed them to the operators' screens while it destroyed the centrifuges underneath. An operator saw a calm, steady process. A data analyst looking at the raw historian would have seen a signal with no noise in it — and real physical processes always have noise. That instinct is a data instinct, and you already have it.

How I will lean on this

Every course in this program has at least one lab built on your data skills rather than on tools you have never opened. The first is in the Labs chapter: pulling Modbus traffic out of a packet capture and using SQL to find the anomalous session. You will be doing familiar work on unfamiliar data — which is the fastest way into a new field.

Your time comes in three shapes. The mistake is treating them the same — trying to start a full lesson in a 15-minute gap, getting nowhere, and feeling like you are failing. You are not; you are using the wrong tool. Here is what each block is genuinely good for.

🕐 15 minutes — retrieval only

Never start new material in 15 minutes. Fifteen minutes is for pulling things back out of your head, which is what actually builds memory.

  • One flashcard deck review (the app's spaced-repetition queue)
  • 5–10 practice questions from a module you finished last week — not this week's
  • Read one case study callout and say out loud what the attacker did, from memory
  • Re-draw the Purdue Model on paper from memory. Ten seconds to draw, and it anchors half of GICSP.
★ ON THE EXAM

Retrieval practice beats re-reading by a wide margin in the research, and the gap widens the longer the delay before the test. Fifteen minutes of quizzing yourself is worth more than forty minutes of highlighting. This is why the short blocks are not the scraps of your study time — they are the engine of it.

You will miss weeks. A child gets sick, a deadline lands, you are simply too tired. The reason study plans fail is almost never the missed week — it is what the missed week does to your sense of whether you are still doing this. So the catch-up plan is written in advance, before you need it, when you are not feeling behind.

📘 DEFINITION

The rule: a missed week is a scheduled event, not a failure. You have four of them per year built into the roadmap already. Using one costs you nothing.

The 10-minute re-entry

Coming back is harder than keeping going, because you have to face how much you think you have forgotten. So the first session back is never new material. It is this, and it takes ten minutes:

  1. Do not re-read anything. Open the flashcard deck for the last module you finished and run it. You will get some wrong. That is the point — it shows you exactly where to aim.
  2. Look at your tracker and read the last line you wrote. Not the whole thing. One line.
  3. Do one lesson quiz you have taken before. Your score will have dropped a little. It comes back within two sessions.

That is it. You are back in. The next session is normal.

Scaling down without stopping

When you can see the week is going badly, drop tiers deliberately rather than just missing sessions:

TierTimeWhat you keep
Full5–7 h/wkEverything — lessons, labs, check-in
Reduced2–3 h/wkLessons + quizzes. Drop the lab; it moves to next week.
Maintenance~45 min/wkFlashcards only. Three 15-minute reviews. No new material at all.
Pause0Declared, with a return date. Tell me the date and I will hold the plan.

Flashcards are where the 15-minute blocks pay off. Two ways to use them: the app's own flashcard screen, or Anki if you want them on your phone during a commute.

📘 DEFINITION

Spaced repetition: reviewing a fact at increasing intervals — a day, then three days, then a week, then a month. Each successful recall pushes the next review further out, so your limited time concentrates on what you are about to forget.

Anki: the standard free spaced-repetition app (desktop, Android free; iOS paid). It imports plain text files.

The import format

Every flashcard set in this program is written as a tab-separated front → back file, which Anki imports directly with no configuration:

📄 ot-ics-m1.txt
What does the C in the CIA triad stand for, and what does it mean?	Confidentiality — only those authorised can read the data
In OT, which letter of the CIA triad usually comes FIRST, and why?	Availability — a control system that stops responding can cause a physical incident; a plant that cannot be controlled is dangerous
What is a compensating control?	A different control used when the intended one is not feasible, giving comparable protection

One tab between front and back, one card per line. In Anki: File → Import → choose the file → Field separator: Tab → Import.

📥 Download the first deck (54 cards)

Covers Security+ Module 1, the exam facts from the roadmap, OT foundations, the safety module and all six case studies. A new deck arrives with each module.

📥 Module 2 deck (32 cards) — threat actors, motivations, vectors and the social-engineering techniques.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

If you paste these into a spreadsheet first, make sure it does not convert the tab into multiple spaces — Anki will then import the whole line as the front of the card with an empty back. Import the .txt directly.

Three rules for cards that actually work

  1. One fact per card. A card asking “list the five Security+ domains” is five cards pretending to be one, and you will keep failing it and feel stupid.
  2. Write the back in your own words wherever you can. A card in my phrasing tests whether you can recognise my phrasing. A card in yours tests whether you understand it.
  3. Make cards ask questions, not show terms. “Modbus” → definition is a weak card. “Which industrial protocol has no authentication at all, so any device on the network can command a PLC?” → “Modbus” is a strong one, because that is the shape the exam and the job both use.
★ ON THE EXAM

Special case — GICSP is open book. For that exam your flashcards do double duty: they become the index you carry in. Start building it from the first GICSP module, not the month before. We will cover how to structure it when we get there, but know now that nothing you write for GICSP is throwaway.

Maps to SY0-701 objectives 1.1 (compare and contrast various types of security controls) and 1.2 (summarize fundamental security concepts). About 30 minutes.

Plain English first

Security has exactly three goals. Everything else in this certification is machinery for achieving one of them.

  1. Keep secrets secret. Only the right people can read the thing.
  2. Keep the truth true. Nobody changed the thing without permission.
  3. Keep it working. The thing is there when you need it.

Those three are called the CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. Nothing to do with the intelligence agency.

And a security control is just a thing you put in place to protect something. A lock. A password rule. A camera. A policy document. A guard. The exam cares less about what controls are than about how you classify them — and it classifies them two different ways at once, which is the single biggest source of lost marks in this domain.

The technical detail

📘 DEFINITION

Confidentiality: information is available only to those authorised. Achieved by encryption, access control, data classification.

Integrity: information has not been altered by anyone unauthorised, and you can prove it. Achieved by hashing, digital signatures, checksums.

Availability: the system is accessible when needed. Achieved by redundancy, backups, failover, capacity planning.

Non-repudiation: the sender cannot later deny having sent it. Achieved by digital signatures and audit logging. Related to integrity but a separate concept — the exam tests this distinction.

Axis 1 — control categories (what kind of thing it is)

CategoryWhat it isExamples
TechnicalImplemented by technologyFirewall, encryption, antivirus, MFA
ManagerialAdministrative — how risk is governedRisk assessments, security policy, vendor reviews
OperationalCarried out by people, day to daySecurity awareness training, guards, change management
PhysicalAffects the physical worldFences, locks, badge readers, bollards, lighting

Axis 2 — control types (what the thing does)

TypeWhat it doesExamples
PreventiveStops it happeningFirewall rule, door lock, MFA
DeterrentDiscourages the attemptWarning sign, visible camera, "prosecution will follow" banner
DetectiveNotices it happenedIDS, log review, motion sensor, audit
CorrectiveFixes it afterwardsRestore from backup, patch, incident response
CompensatingStands in when the intended control is not feasibleExtra monitoring on a server that cannot be patched
DirectiveTells people what to doAcceptable use policy, posted procedure
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake that costs people marks: treating these as one list. They are two independent axes, and every control has a value on both.

A security guard is physical (category) and simultaneously deterrent, preventive and detective (type). A camera is physical and both deterrent and detective. Read the question to see which axis it wants. “Which category?” wants technical/managerial/operational/physical. “Which type?” wants preventive/deterrent/detective/corrective/compensating/directive.

🏭 The real-world OT example

🏭 IN THE PLANT

A water treatment plant doses chlorine into drinking water. Too little and pathogens survive; too much and you injure the people drinking it. The dosing setpoint lives in a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) — a ruggedised industrial computer that reads sensors and drives pumps and valves.

Now place the controls:

You asked for TRITON in depth. To understand why it is the most frightening ICS attack yet seen, you first need to understand what it attacked — so we build the Safety Instrumented System first, then break it.

Plain English first

Every dangerous industrial process has two separate control systems, and the separation is the whole point.

  1. The control system runs the process day to day. It holds the reactor at 300°C, keeps the tank at 60% full, runs the pumps. It is trying to make the plant work.
  2. The safety system does nothing at all, almost all the time. It watches, and if things go badly wrong it shuts the process down safely. It is trying to make the plant not kill anyone.

They are separate on purpose. If the control system fails — or is compromised — the safety system is supposed to be untouched and still able to stop the process. It is the last automated line before physical relief valves and emergency response.

📘 DEFINITION

SIS (Safety Instrumented System): an independent system of sensors, logic solver and final elements that takes a process to a safe state when defined limits are exceeded.

SIF (Safety Instrumented Function): one specific protective action, e.g. “if pressure exceeds 12 bar, close valve XV-101.”

Logic solver: the safety-rated controller that decides — the SIS equivalent of a PLC. Triconex is a well-known family.

SIL (Safety Integrity Level) 1–4: how reliable a SIF must be. Higher SIL = lower permitted probability of failure on demand. SIL 3 is common for serious hazards; SIL 4 is rare and very expensive.

IEC 61511 / ISA 84: the standard governing SIS for the process industries — essentially the same document, ISA 84 being the US adoption. IEC 61508 is the parent standard for the equipment itself.

The technical detail: why an SIS is different

PropertyBasic control system (BPCS)Safety system (SIS)
JobKeep the process running wellTake the process to a safe state
Normal stateConstantly actingDoing nothing, watching
Failure modeFails in whatever directionFails safe — loss of signal trips the process
Change controlRoutine engineering changeFormal, documented, often requires a physical key switch
CertificationNone requiredCertified to a SIL under IEC 61508/61511
Independence—Must be independent of the BPCS — separate sensors, separate logic, separate final elements
★ ON THE EXAM

In RUN, the logic cannot be changed over the network. Changing safety logic is supposed to require someone to physically walk to the cabinet and turn a key. That is a deliberately analogue defence against exactly this attack.

Three names for the same malware: TRITON (FireEye), TRISIS (Dragos), HatMan (US CISA/ICS-CERT). All the same thing.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

From memory, not verified this session. The account below reflects the widely-published analyses. The narrative is well corroborated across vendors and government reporting, but I could not re-check specifics today.

  1. Target: a petrochemical facility in Saudi Arabia, discovered 2017.
  2. Entry and traversal: the attackers got into the IT network, then crossed to the OT network, and eventually reached an engineering workstation used to program the Triconex safety controllers. Note that they did not attack the SIS from the internet — they attacked the computer that is allowed to talk to it. That is the pattern.
  3. The opening they used: the key switch on the target controller had reportedly been left in PROGRAM rather than RUN. The analogue defence was there and was not engaged.
  4. What the malware did: it implanted a backdoor into the safety controller's firmware, giving the attackers the ability to read and write the safety logic at will — in effect, the power to decide whether the plant's last automated protection would function.
  5. How it was found: the attackers made a mistake. Their code did not match what the controller expected, and the Triconex failed safe and tripped the plant. Twice. The operator investigated an unexplained shutdown and found the malware.

Why this is the line-crossing attack. Stuxnet destroyed machines. Ukraine turned off the lights. TRITON is the first known malware built to disable the system whose only job is to stop people dying.

It only has value to an attacker in combination with a second attack on the process itself: you neutralise the protection, then you cause the over-pressure. The intended outcome of that combination is an explosion or toxic release, with the safeguards intentionally disabled.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

This is your lab. Everything so far has been learning someone else's tools; this one is you doing what you already do well, on data that happens to come from a plant.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The premise: OT traffic is repetitive to a degree office traffic never is. An HMI polls a PLC every 500 ms, using the same function codes, for the same registers, for years. That means a baseline is genuinely achievable — and once you have one, anomalies are obvious rather than buried. This is why baselining works in OT and barely works in IT, and it is the single most marketable thing in this whole program for you.

Step 1 — get traffic worth analysing

Leave the Lab 01 rig running for 20–30 minutes with a script polling the PLC on a fixed interval, so you have a realistic baseline. Then, in the last two minutes, do three “suspicious” things from a second workstation VM:

  • read a register range nobody normally reads
  • issue a write (function code 6 or 16) from a host that only ever reads
  • poll at a noticeably different interval

Step 2 — turn packets into rows

This is the step that converts a security problem into a data problem:

zeek -r lab02.pcap
# produces conn.log, modbus.log and others

# Zeek logs are tab-separated with a header block.
# Strip the headers and load into SQLite:
cat modbus.log | grep -v '^#' > modbus.tsv
sqlite3 ot.db
.mode tabs
.import modbus.tsv modbus_raw

Now you have a table. You are home.

Step 3 — the queries

Four queries. Each one corresponds to a real detection used in production OT monitoring.

a) Who talks to whom? (the asset relationship baseline)

SELECT src_ip, dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS msgs,
       MIN(ts) AS first_seen, MAX(ts) AS last_seen
FROM   modbus_raw
GROUP  BY src_ip, dst_ip
ORDER  BY msgs DESC;

A plant network has a short list here. A new pair appearing is one of the highest-value alerts in all of OT security.

b) Who writes, and did they ever write before?

SELECT src_ip,
       SUM(CASE WHEN func LIKE '%READ%'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reads,
       SUM(CASE WHEN func LIKE '%WRITE%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS writes
FROM   modbus_raw
GROUP  BY src_ip
HAVING writes > 0;

Most hosts should have zero writes. An HMI writes; a historian never should. A host whose write count goes from 0 to 1 is the whole ballgame.

c) Did the polling rhythm change? (the window function)

WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT src_ip, ts,
         ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY src_ip ORDER BY ts) AS gap
  FROM   modbus_raw
)
SELECT src_ip,
       ROUND(AVG(gap),3)  AS avg_gap,
       ROUND(MIN(gap),3)  AS min_gap,
       ROUND(MAX(gap),3)  AS max_gap,
       COUNT(*)           AS samples
FROM   gaps
WHERE  gap IS NOT NULL
GROUP  BY src_ip;

A legitimate poller has a tiny spread between min and max. A wide spread, or a sudden change in the average, suggests something else is generating the traffic.

d) The one that matters most — writes outside a change window

CREATE TABLE approved_changes (
  host TEXT, window_start REAL, window_end REAL, ticket TEXT
);

SELECT m.ts, m.src_ip, m.dst_ip, m.func
FROM   modbus_raw m
LEFT   JOIN approved_changes c
       ON  m.src_ip = c.host
       AND m.ts BETWEEN c.window_start AND c.window_end
WHERE  m.func LIKE '%WRITE%'
  AND  c.ticket IS NULL;
🏭 IN THE PLANT

That last query is a left join keeping the unmatched rows — the first anti-join you ever learned. In a plant it means: every command that changed something, with no approved change record behind it. Commercial OT security platforms sell this as a headline feature. You just wrote it in eight lines, and you understand exactly what it does and where it would produce false positives. That understanding is what they are hiring.

Step 4 — write it up honestly

In “what surprised me”, address the thing a good interviewer will probe: how many false positives did these produce, and what would you do about them? The answer for query (d) is usually “a lot, until the change-management data is trustworthy” — and noticing that detection quality is downstream of data quality is a genuinely senior observation.

The layer that stops it is the interlock wired independently of the PLC. Say so in your write-up — it shows you know the difference between detecting and preventing, which is the difference between a monitoring analyst and an engineer.

Module 1 was about what you protect and how. This module is about who is coming, why, and through which door. Three questions, and the exam asks all three in disguise:

  1. Who? A bored teenager and a foreign intelligence service are both “attackers”, but you would not defend against them the same way. The exam calls the who a threat actor.
  2. Why? Money, politics, revenge, ideology, or simply orders from a government. The exam calls this motivation, and it is what lets you predict what an attacker will do next.
  3. Through which door? Every way in — an email, a USB stick, a vendor's laptop, a phone call — is a threat vector. The sum of all your doors is your attack surface.

The single most useful idea in the module: match the actor to the door. A nation-state will find a door you did not know you had. Organised crime walks through the one you left unlocked. Knowing which you face tells you where to spend.

The technical detail: threat actors

The exam describes each actor on three attributes. Learn the attributes, not just the names, because questions describe an actor by attribute and ask you to name it.

📘 DEFINITION

Internal vs external: does the actor already have legitimate access (an employee, a contractor) or not?

Resources / funding: from pocket money to a national budget. Determines how long they can keep trying and what tools they can afford or build.

Sophistication / capability: from running a downloaded tool to writing malware that speaks a grid protocol natively.

Two traps in this table.

Insider threat does not mean malicious. The exam includes the well-meaning employee who plugs in a found USB stick. If a question says “unintentional” and “employee”, the answer is still insider threat.

Shadow IT is on the actor list but is not an adversary. A question asking which “threat actor” is represented by a department running its own unapproved cloud file share is looking for shadow IT. Do not talk yourself out of it because nobody meant harm.

Pretexting vs impersonation. Impersonation is who the attacker claims to be. Pretexting is the story that makes the claim work. They usually travel together; if a question stresses the fabricated scenario, the answer is pretexting. If it stresses the false identity, impersonation.

🏭 The real-world OT example

🏭 IN THE PLANT

Put the whole module on one incident. Ukraine, December 2015:

  • Actor: nation-state — very high resources, very high sophistication, patient (months inside before acting).
  • Motivation: service disruption, in the context of war.
  • Vector in: message-based — spear-phishing emails with a file-based payload (a document with a malicious macro).
  • Vector across: stolen credentials on the utility's own remote-access tools — a door that was there on purpose.
  • Attack surface abused: the connection between the business network and the control network, which existed so engineers could work remotely.

Every row of this module's tables appears in one real attack. That is why Domain 2 is 22% of the exam and why GICSP asks about the same incident again in more depth.

🦺 SAFETY & ENVIRONMENT

Three actors, three physical outcomes.

Insider (Maroochy, 2000): a disgruntled ex-contractor with a stolen radio and insider knowledge — low resources, high system knowledge, motivation revenge — released about 800,000 litres of raw sewage. The vector was unsecure wireless.

Organised crime (Colonial, 2021): financial gain via ransomware. Vector: a legacy VPN account without MFA — an unsupported, unsecured door. The pipeline stopped even though OT was never touched.

Nation-state (TRITON, 2017): the safety system itself, through an engineering workstation. The vector chain ran IT → OT → the one machine allowed to talk to the safety controller. When the actor is this sophisticated, the attack surface is every path to the thing that matters.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Attack surface is a query. “Every open port on every device, joined to the asset inventory, where the port is not on the approved-services list” is an attack-surface report, and it is a left join with a null check — the same shape as Lab 03.
